title: Private fields (#), getters, setters, and symbols
hook: JavaScript had no real private instance fields for decades — only conventions and closures. Hash-prefixed private fields (#) are enforced by the engine. TypeScript private and C# private are not the same thing, and interviews love that distinction.

blocks.text: **Private fields** use the `#` prefix: `#token` is stored per instance and cannot be read or written from outside the class body. **Getters and setters** (`get size() / set size(v)`) are accessor properties — they look like fields but run functions. **Symbols** provide unique keys that are omitted from normal enumeration but are not true privacy — anyone with the symbol reference can access the property.

entries.plainDefinition: Instance storage prefixed with #, accessible only inside the class declaration. Enforced at runtime by the engine.
Pre-# pattern: store private data in a WeakMap keyed by the public instance.
Property defined with get/set keywords; descriptor uses getter/setter functions instead of value.
Factory function keeps variables in closure scope — invisible outside the factory.
entries.example: `function createCounter() { let n = 0; return { inc() { n++; } }; }`

blocks.text: Encapsulation protects invariants — a session object should not let callers set `expiresAt` to the past. C# enforces `private` through Common Language Runtime (CLR) metadata. TypeScript `private` is a compile-time check that **erases** in the JavaScript bundle — users can still read the property at runtime. JavaScript `#fields` are **real runtime privacy** per instance, though not as rich as CLR access levels (no protected, internal, or friend assemblies).

blocks.title: Three different "private" meanings
blocks.body: C# private: CLR enforced. TypeScript private: compile-time only. JavaScript #field: engine enforced on the instance. Underscore `_secret`: convention only — not enforced.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Lexical class binding
items.body: Private names are resolved lexically to the class body — subclasses cannot access `#parentField` unless it is in their own class declaration scope.

items.title: Per-instance storage
items.body: Each instance gets its own # slots — not on the prototype. Access outside the class throws TypeError.

items.title: Not in JSON.stringify
items.body: Private fields are not enumerable own properties in the traditional sense — they do not appear in spread or JSON output.

items.title: Getters expose controlled views
items.body: Public `get tokenPreview()` can return a redacted string while `#token` stays hidden.

snippet.label: Private fields and public accessors
snippet.explanation: Line 2–3: # fields initialized per instance. Line 10–16: getters expose computed views without leaking #token. Line 18–21: method mutates private state with invariant check. Line 26: syntax error if accessing # outside class body.

snippet.label: TypeScript private versus JavaScript #
snippet.explanation: Line 3: TS private does not hide key in bundle unless you use # or WeakMap. Line 4: # survives emit as real privacy. Line 11–12: critical interview point — DevTools can read TS private after compile.

snippet.label: Symbol keys — unique but not private
snippet.explanation: Line 1: symbol is unique. Line 5: stored as computed property. Line 12: omitted from Object.keys but accessible with symbol reference — not security.

snippet.label: WeakMap pattern before # fields
snippet.explanation: Line 1: module-scoped WeakMap holds private bag. Line 4: associate data with instance without own properties. Line 12: still bypassable if internals map is exported — pattern not cryptographic privacy.

blocks.title: Treating underscore prefix as private
blocks.body: `this._token` is a public own property — any code can read it. Linters may warn but the engine does not enforce.

blocks.title: Subclass accessing parent # fields
blocks.body: Private fields are not inherited for access — `class B extends A` cannot read `#field` from A. Use protected patterns via composition or protected-like getters in the parent.

blocks.text: Private fields use **internal slots** checked lexically at access sites — the spec uses `#` in parse tree, not string names. **Private methods** `#helper()` follow the same rules. **Brand checks**: only code in the class body can read `#x` on instances of that class — including on other instances of the same class (`other.#token` inside Session is allowed). DevTools in modern browsers may still inspect some internal state through debugging APIs — privacy is about language access, not anti-tamper security. For **true secrets** (API keys), never ship them to the client bundle — no access modifier fixes that.

blocks.title: When to use which pattern
rows: API surface during development — pair with # for runtime

snippet.label: Failure mode — TS private in production bundle
snippet.explanation: Line 4: TS private becomes public property in JS output. Line 9: any script on the page can read refreshToken. Strong answer: use # or server-side storage for secrets.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Equating TypeScript private with C# private or JavaScript # — three different mechanisms. Claiming Symbol properties are secure private fields — they are hidden from enumeration, not from code with the symbol. Saying JSON.stringify can leak # fields — it does not; but TS private fields without # do serialize if public on the object.

interviewTakeaways: JavaScript # fields are runtime-enforced per instance; TypeScript private erases unless you use # in emit.
C# private is CLR metadata enforcement — richest access model of the three.
Symbols and WeakMaps are obscurity patterns, not substitutes for # or CLR private.

60s: Three privates — C# CLR runtime, TS compile-time only, JS # engine slots. Underscore is convention. Symbols skip enumeration but are not secret. Use # for real instance privacy in modern JS classes.
Follow-up: can a subclass read a parent # field?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'TypeScript private equals C# private.' Strong: TS erases; C# enforces at runtime; JS # enforces per class lexical scope.
Using _prefix expecting enforcement — still a public property.
Symbol keys for security — export the symbol and privacy collapses.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TS private is erased in emit — use # private fields when runtime hiding matters.
C# private enforced by metadata; JS has no protected/internal assembly scopes.
